I want you to solve GitHub issue #3757: implement the fix, validate it,
commit it, and report. Read this entire brief, then the repository AGENTS.md
and its relevant routed guidance. Do not stop at a survey or plan. If the issue
and repository genuinely leave a decision open, ask the judge one specific
question and wait for the answer, then continue.

# Working agreement

Your repository is the `bifrost` checkout under /workspace in your own container
(`ls /workspace/*/bifrost` finds it). The judge is Claude Fable.
All competing lanes receive this identical brief. Do not inspect other lanes,
their sessions, the judge's private files, or evaluation results about this issue.
Before investigation, verify your checkout has no tracked or untracked changes
and is checked out detached at this exact commit: 0722dea6bcb52ef5335695a701631d157c31cbf4
Do not fetch from origin or any other remote.
The detached checkout is explicitly authorized for this evaluation. Report its
full hash. Do not merge newer master or change the base during your initial run.

History rule. Work only from the base commit above. Do not log, show, diff, check
out or otherwise read any commit, branch or tag that is not an ancestor of the base,
and do not use gh, the GitHub API or the web for this issue, its comments, timeline
or pull requests: the issue text in this brief is complete.

Work only in your container. Commit your changes on the detached HEAD, with
real messages. Do not push, create branches or PRs, edit issue labels, or post
GitHub comments. The judge exports your commits. Commit all intended work before
your final report; never stage unrelated files or use git add -A.
Do not write to any memory directory or MEMORY.md: that pool is shared across
sessions and harnesses. Keep discoveries in your report. Do not read other
evaluation sessions or their reports. Do not launch subagents; do the entire
solution in this lane, so every configuration has the same delegation policy.

Use plain cargo and the repository testing guidance. Clear JAVA_HOME and set
BIFROST_PARALLELISM=1 and RAYON_NUM_THREADS=1. Let nextest own concurrency;
pass --max-fail 100. Run relevant crate and integration suites. Changes under a
language's graph code or analysis usages require that language's usage and issue
suites plus cargo nextest run --max-fail 100 -p brokk-bifrost-analysis --lib.
Run cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings and
format changed files. Do not reduce nextest concurrency without measured resource
exhaustion. Report pre-existing failures only after checking the same base.
The harness fails a turn after 10 minutes without activity, so never block on
one command for longer than 5 minutes: run long builds and suites in the
background or with a timeout of at most 300000 ms and poll their output.
No notification arrives between turns: never end your turn to wait for a
background command, because nothing will wake you. Poll it yourself in the
foreground, in waits of at most 5 minutes, and keep the turn running until the
FINAL REPORT is written.
Never run shared-cache GC or delete another session's build targets. If disk
pressure requires isolated storage, use the repository's managed target helper.
If the build cache wrapper stalls (a cargo command that starts no compiler for
more than ten minutes), you may run that command through plain cargo
(/usr/local/cargo/bin/cargo) and say so in your report; do not move target/
or change shared cache settings.

Fix causes with tree-sitter and analyzer structures, not source-text parsing or
regex fallbacks. Use assertions for construction invariants, iterative traversal
for deep trees, plain ASCII, and the existing shared helpers. Demonstrate a
production-shaped regression failing before and passing after the fix.
Read relevant architecture chapters before changing identities, cache, usage,
dataflow, semantic models or results. Bump the language extraction epoch when
the persisted language facts change; do not bump it for query-only changes.
Use an ExecPlan under .agents/plans only when the reposi

dels for Rust std and framework inputs: `std::env::args`/`var`, stdin, HTTP headers, and Axum/Actix handler extractors (`Query<T>`, `Path<T>`, `Json<T>`), including handler parameters as entry points.
2. **SQL API contracts.** Reviewed models for SQLx, Diesel, rusqlite, postgres, and tokio-postgres. Separate the SQL text operand from bound values, and support generic, async, trait, and callback forms. A complete sink model must let analysis observe the SQL text at the call without the library body, and must leave unrelated effects open.
3. **Caller completeness at modeled boundaries.** A procedure whose only unknowns are modeled calls should get complete semantics. Confirm or refute the "likely" root cause above.
4. **Rust value construction.** `format!`, `+`/`push_str`, builders, closures, async fns, and trait-object dispatch.
5. **Shipped policy.** A general Rust request-to-SQL security policy that uses these models, so users do not have to write endpoint models for common libraries.

Keep the sound result contract: missing models stay visibly incomplete, with a diagnostic that names the missing model or capability. An empty result from incomplete discovery is never a clean result.

## Acceptance criteria

- A documented support matrix: the supported Rust sources, SQL sinks, sanitizers, and propagation shapes, and which remain incomplete.
- Positive fixtures: a proven source-to-SQL-text path with a complete run.
- Negative fixtures (parameterized, non-reaching, sanitized): proven no-flow with a complete run.
- The three-case sample above passes as a regression test, plus independent cases for each supported API family.
- The rerun CodeQL comparison on the sample gives matching complete results. Stretch goal: a real Rust web service with SQL.

## Related

- #3412: declared-storage Rust endpoint contracts (direct overlap on the store-based slice)
- #3678: Rust sysroot summary binding
- #1877: external-code activation and completeness
- #2705: Rust container/std summaries
- Background: #1871, #2596, #2519, #1951

The managed build has a live Rust compiler process and is continuing normally; it is a cold rebuild caused by the missing target cache, not a wrapper stall. I’m letting this focused run finish, then subsequent checks should reuse the rebuilt target.

The active pack is now visible in the resolver: the exact modeled receiver is `postgres.client.Client`, with a unique public `execute` declaration and complete summary. I’m adding a structured receiver-type proof to external dispatch so flow binds that same owner/member/receiver/arity tuple instead of treating the method as an unknown local call; the focused rerun is compiling this change now.

The regression now gets past pack activation and confirms the declaration and complete summary are published under the expected model owner. The remaining failure was exact external call resolution for value-receiver Rust methods; that is the root binding gap I’m fixing. The managed compiler has been waiting in its cache shim for several minutes, so I’m monitoring it against the brief’s 10-minute fallback threshold.

The managed Cargo shim has now spent over 10 minutes waiting on `mbx-rustc` without starting `rustc`, meeting the brief’s explicit fallback condition. I’m stopping that stalled invocation and will rerun this same focused command through `/usr/local/cargo/bin/cargo`; I’ll record the fallback in the final validation report.

The raw-Cargo fallback compiled far enough to catch two implementation issues: a `Box<str>` comparison and a temporary borrow in the exact receiver-type lookup. Both are corrected. The focused rerun is rebuilding the analyzer with those fixes; no production result has been accepted until this run passes.

The analyzer now compiles with exact receiver-model resolution and the std type-fact changes. Cargo is linking the suite’s required binaries and integration target; once the regression executes I’ll address any remaining semantic gap before broadening validation.

The method proof code now compiles, but the focused run still reports the call as unresolved, so the proof is returning no exact receiver target. I’m narrowing this to the typed receiver lookup versus the external model admission check and reducing the regression’s failure output to the completion and diagnostics that matter.

The model metadata and receiver type are now being traced at the exact external-dispatch boundary. The current failure still names only `src/api.rs::execute`; I’m adding one narrow trace of the resolver status for calls in that fixture file, since the receiver-model path is not being entered at all.

The trace revealed the resolver status that blocked the proof: for `client.execute`, Rust reports `Resolved` to the lexical receiver binding, with the focus range on the member name. The external-model fallback only ran for `NoDefinition` and `UnresolvableImportBoundary`, so it never examined a receiver whose value was resolved but whose method was not. I’m extending the exact fallback to that narrowly typed case: a resolved lexical receiver with no callable definitions, followed by an exact model-backed receiver-type and method proof.

I’ve changed the fallback gate to accept only that receiver-only result (`Resolved`, no callable declarations, and a lexical receiver), then independently prove the concrete model type and exact callable shape. The regression rebuild is progressing; if the proof binds, the test will also show whether the modeled call closes cleanup and caller coverage as intended.

The receiver-only gate still did not enter the model path, which means the resolver returned one or more declaration candidates alongside `Resolved`. I’m capturing those candidate facts now; the next change will allow the model fallback only when the receiver’s exact external model identity proves the same concrete type and callable, so local declarations cannot be displaced by spelling alone.

The latest compile is running through the normal repository Cargo shim (the earlier cache stall has cleared), and it has built the analyzer plus downstream crates so far. The added resolver trace will show whether the `Resolved` result includes a method definition or only the receiver binding.

The build is past analyzer compilation but the cache shim is handling several test-binary compiler actions; those actions currently have no child `rustc`, so I’m watching for the same stall pattern. The already-built analysis changes are clean; the remaining work is identifying the resolver candidates and completing the end-to-end proof.

The three `mbx-rustc` wrappers for the suite binaries are waiting without child compilers, while the analysis and downstream crates have already compiled. I’ll apply the same 10-minute cache-stall threshold to these actions, then use the raw Cargo fallback if they remain blocked.

The suite binary cache actions have now waited about seven minutes without launching compiler children; the command is still below the brief’s 10-minute fallback point. The core implementation build succeeded, and I’m keeping this invocation alive until the threshold or completion.

The latest trace corrected my earlier hypothesis: `client.execute` does resolve to a method declaration, but that declaration is inside the indexed `postgres` stub crate. The external-model bridge currently treats resolved declarations as local, so it skips the reviewed model. I’m tightening the proof around that exact dependency declaration and will use the three case outcomes to distinguish call-model closure from any remaining caller-completeness gap.

The proof now starts from the resolver’s single Rust declaration, checks its structured package/type/member identity against an activated public callable, and only then treats the modeled boundary as complete. I’ve removed the trace instrumentation and the focused regression is compiling against that path.

The cache wrapper has held `mbx-rustc` without launching a real compiler for over ten minutes. I’m stopping that stalled invocation and switching this validation command to `/usr/local/cargo/bin/cargo`, as the brief permits; I’ll report the fallback.

The plain Cargo fallback is now doing real compilation (`rustc` is active on `brokk-bifrost-analysis`). This fresh fallback rebuild is substantially slower than an incremental test run, so I’m letting it finish before I adjust any further source code against compiler feedback.

The fallback build succeeded. The first runtime check reached the new proof, then hit an internal invariant: the identity carried by the proof is `postgres.client.Client.execute`, but the call-relation validator could not recover that identity from the proof’s canonical name. I’m aligning the exact proof representation with the existing validator before rerunning the fixture.

The structured trace confirms the reviewed callable and its complete summary are both selected (`Unique`, complete summary). The remaining gap is exactly the external receiver-dispatch closure: flow requires the summary to claim `covers_overrides` before it can close this call’s coverage. These are concrete inherent methods on the modeled structs, so I’m making that claim only for the two reviewed SQL methods and checking that the complete positive and negative results then follow.

The generator’s release-tooling build is still active; it is rebuilding the large analysis dependency under this Cargo target configuration. The core implementation compiled on the prior run, and I’m waiting for this one to produce the updated reviewed pack before retesting the result-closure behavior.

The caller trace now shows that the SQL driver call closes in the summary-backed tier. A different call remains open in `helper_c.rs`: the sample’s `"…".to_owned()` conversion. I’m tracing that call’s resolved type and callable identity so the regression keeps the issue’s actual construction shape and the support matrix can distinguish verified from unsupported construction forms.

The judge confirmed the required direction. The SQL model now closes the exact `Client.execute` boundary, but the three-case regression still has an unmodeled call in `helper_c.rs`; I’m tracing that structured call next, then I’ll finish the required source contracts, matrix, and validation.

The exact SQL boundary is now being recognized as a complete modeled call, including the receiver dispatch. The trace is rebuilding the analysis crates after that change; once the regression runs, it will tell us whether the blocker is the sample’s `to_owned()` conversion or a separate semantic gap.

The remaining blocker is confirmed: `helper_c.rs` has one unresolved `.to_owned()` call on the sample’s string literal; the SQL call itself is covered by the reviewed model. I’m adding a narrow, structured `&str`/`ToOwned::to_owned` contract so the original sample shape can remain intact, with the resolver refusing the prelude proof when the call shape or import evidence is ambiguous.

I’ve added a reviewed `ToOwned` flow summary and a resolver gate that recognizes only literal receivers with an unambiguous prelude/import surface. The sample test now activates both the Rust std conversion pack and the SQL-driver pack. I’m regenerating the checked-in std pack so its shipping audit remains reproducible.

The `ToOwned` routing compiles far enough to catch and correct a Rust ownership error in the new import check. The pack generator is rebuilding the analysis dependency now; after it completes, I’ll rerun the one failing regression before adding the source endpoint contracts.

The std pack now ships the new 10th summary and the shipping check distinguishes its one receiver call from the existing receiverless conversions. The regression rebuild is still running; it now compiles the full policy integration target, so I’m letting nextest’s default concurrency finish before inspecting the new proof trace.

The resolver was intentionally preserving `Incomplete` before it asked the exact external-model path for evidence. I’ve narrowed the bridge so an incomplete Rust lookup can be upgraded only when that helper proves the AST call, external owner, public callable, and active summary; unresolved cases keep their original diagnostic. The regression is rebuilding against this bridge now.

The new exact fallback still isn’t closing the sample call, so I’ve added temporary stage-level trace points to the `ToOwned` binding path. This should separate a model activation problem from an import or AST proof rejection; I’ll use that evidence to make the final narrow adjustment and remove the traces.

The model proof now reaches the exact `ToOwned` declaration, but the coverage trace still labels one `helper_c.rs` invoke unknown. I’m checking the call-site identity against the resolver proof to determine whether that invoke is `.to_owned()` or the local helper call, since the correct fix differs.

The trace identifies the `helper_c.rs` invoke as the literal’s `to_owned()` call. The exact resolver helper already proves its std model, but the shared call-dispatch wrapper only offered `NoDefinition` and `UnresolvableImportBoundary` to language model expansion. I’ve allowed Rust `Incomplete` through that same exact-proof gate; unrelated or unmodeled calls still fail the proof and remain incomplete.

The call-dispatch change is through the crate rebuild and the policy integration binary is still linking. The regression’s remaining work will then be quick; I’ll immediately inspect the positive and negative completion outcomes.

One more adjustment promotes the exact, model-proven Rust boundary to the external-boundary state the shared dataflow resolver understands. The promotion is conditional on the resolver having produced the exact external proof; ordinary incomplete calls remain unresolved. The focused run is compiling this final route now.

The trace confirmed the semantic Invoke is `.to_owned()`, not the cross-file helper call. The call-graph bridge alone cannot close it because Rust’s semantic lowering independently decides whether an external method has a complete summary. I’m wiring the same literal and unshadowed-prelude proof into that lowering, including the modeled `String` return type needed to prove `let _` cleanup is drop-free.

I’ve confirmed the right layer for the `to_owned()` gap: Rust semantic lowering must recognize the same exact standard method and its `String` return, because that lowering owns both the call coverage and destructor evidence. The std pack regeneration is compiling that implementation now.

The analyzer crate is still compiling the whole changed Rust lowering unit. The active `rustc` process is using CPU, so this is a slow build rather than a cache stall. The std summary now declares `ToOwned::to_owned`’s owned `String` result, which is the destructor fact the sample’s ignored return needs.

The updated std pack regenerated cleanly: 10 candidates, 10 shipped summaries, zero rejects. The three-case regression is now rebuilding with the semantic-lowering hook and the explicit `String` return signature; nextest will provide the first end-to-end confirmation of the cleanup and caller-completeness path.

The analysis and policy crates have compiled; the root integration-test executable is still linking. The first point of uncertainty was the std method’s argument type and exact receiver proof; both are now present in the shipped pack and Rust lowering, so the upcoming result will test the intended complete path rather than the earlier partial model.

The focused regression build session ended before I could retrieve its result. I’m checking whether the test completed, then I’ll rerun it with output captured and continue with the remaining source models, family coverage, and required validation.

The SQL driver model now resolves the exact stub method and contributes the required six conservative transfers. The remaining failure is specifically that snapshot discovery still retains a call-resolution gap after those transfers are applied; I’m tracing which completeness predicate fails so the fix closes only the modeled call boundary.

The structured trace confirms the judge’s hypothesis on this base: the SQL call has a complete exact model and six bindable transfers, yet the caller snapshot remains open because the model is not allowed to discharge its call-resolution refinement. I’m narrowing the change to that exact authored boundary; unmodeled or incomplete calls will keep their existing gap.

The PostgreSQL three-case regression now reaches a closed, summary-backed verdict; the temporary debug run showed one definite positive and complete coverage. I’ve added the same three-case fixture against the reviewed rusqlite model so both shipped API families get independent production-path coverage. The suite is rebuilding after the instrumentation cleanup.

The first complete-discovery trace exposed a second independent issue: the path exists, but `String + &str` still carries an unknown operator-dispatch proof, so the finding is downgraded to possible. I’ve added a structured, narrow proof for concatenation chains rooted in the exact modeled string-literal `to_owned()` call; other overloaded operators remain incomplete.
I’m resuming at validation. The managed Cargo target path disappeared between runs, so I’m checking the repository’s target helper and current working tree before restarting the required suites.

The managed Cargo shim restored the target link and the clean rebuild is progressing through the analysis crate. The focused regression command is still running; I’m letting nextest retain its default worker count.

The shim restored the managed target, but the analysis compiler child has made no progress for about 15 minutes and is blocked on an inode lock inside the cache wrapper. I’m checking whether that lock releases; I won’t inspect or alter the shared cache or other sessions.

The direct Cargo retry is now compiling instead of waiting on the cache lock, using the same managed `target/` location and no target override. Several workspace crates have rebuilt; the SQL regression test binary is not ready yet.
